deep.reconstruction:
The page has two blocks separated by a horizontal rule.

BLOCK A: reducing the Legendre integral to a quartic with roots on the unit circle.

(A1) Riemann starts from K-type integrals F(a) = ∫_0^a dy / (√(1−y²) √(1−k²y²)).
- He substitutes y → 1/y. Then 1−y² → (y²−1)/y² and 1−k²/y² → (y²−k²)/y², with √(y²−k²) = k √(y²/k² − 1). This gives F(a) = −∫_∞^{1/a} (dy/k) / (√(y²−1) √(y²/k² − 1)).
- He then substitutes y → k y. This gives F(a) = −∫_∞^{1/(ak)} dy / √((y²−1)(k²y²−1)) = ∫_{1/(ak)}^∞ dy / √((1−y²)(1−k²y²)).
- Combined, this is invariance of the differential dy/√((1−y²)(1−k²y²)) under the involution y ↦ 1/(ky), up to sign.

(A2) Fixed points. Riemann writes a = −1/(ak), i.e. the involution y ↦ −1/(ky), which also preserves the quartic up to sign. Its fixed points are a = ± i/√k.

(A3) A Möbius map sending the fixed points to 0 and ∞. With c = i/√k he writes (y − c) z = c (y + c), i.e. z = c (y+c)/(y−c).
- Equivalently −i√k z = (y+c)/(y−c).
- Because the matrix [[c, c²], [1, −c]] has trace 0, this map is an involution. So the inverse has the same form: −i√k y = (z+c)/(z−c). Riemann writes exactly this.

(A4) Images of the branch points ±1, ±1/k. The lines '(z − c) ± c(z + c)…', 'z(1+c) − c(1−c)' and the sign marks '− − +' are scratch work for this. My completion: put w = −i√k z = (y+c)/(y−c). Since c is purely imaginary for k > 0, |1+c| = |1−c|. Hence
- w(1) = (1+c)/(1−c) = e^{iφ},
- w(−1) = e^{−iφ},
- w(1/k) = −e^{−iφ},
- w(−1/k) = −e^{iφ}.

Here φ = 2 arctan(1/√k). Riemann's result is the quartic (z − e^{φi})(z − e^{−φi})(z + e^{φi})(z + e^{−φi}) = z⁴ − 2cos(2φ) z² + 1. This is invariant under z → −z and z → 1/z. So the Legendre integral with real modulus becomes, up to a constant factor, ∫ dz/√(z⁴ − 2cos2φ z² + 1).

BLOCK B: a conformal map by an elliptic integral and the equation Δu = μ²u.

(B1) He defines x + yi = ∫_0^{p+qi} dz / √((z−e^{ψi})(z−e^{−ψi})(z+e^{ψi})(z+e^{−ψi})).
- Substituting z² → z (my step), this becomes, up to a factor 1/2 and with the angle doubled, x + yi = ∫^{re^{φi}} dz / √(z (z−e^{ψi})(z−e^{−ψi})).
- This is a Schwarz–Christoffel-type elliptic map from the z-plane (polar coordinates r, φ) to the (x, y)-plane.

(B2) He transforms the equation ∂²u/∂x² + ∂²u/∂y² = μ²u into the coordinates log r, φ.
- Since log r + φi = log z is analytic in x + yi, Δ_{xy} u = (u_{log r, log r} + u_{φφ}) · (d log z/dζ)(conjugate), with ζ = x + yi.
- We have d log z/dζ = √((z−e^{ψi})(z−e^{−ψi})/z).
- Using |z − e^{±ψi}|² = r² − 2r cos(φ ∓ ψ) + 1, this gives (u_{ll} + u_{φφ}) · √(r² − 2cos(φ+ψ) r + 1) √(r² − 2cos(φ−ψ) r + 1) / r = μ²u. This is Riemann's line, and it is correct.

(B3) To solve for u_{ll} + u_{φφ} = μ²u · r / (|1 − re^{i(φ+ψ)}| |1 − re^{i(φ−ψ)}|), he expands the reciprocal factor as r times a product of four binomial series of type (1 − e^{(φ+ψ)i} r)^{−1/2}, with exponents ±(φ+ψ) and ±(φ−ψ).
- The series is (1−x)^{−1/2} = Σ (−1)^n Π(−1/2) / (Πn Π(−1/2−n)) x^n = Σ Π(n−1/2) / (Πn Π(−1/2)) x^n, where Π is Gauss's factorial, Π(s) = Γ(s+1). This is valid for r < 1.

(B4) For collecting terms in the fourfold product he introduces the linear system
- n1 + n2 + n3 + n4 = m1 (total power of r),
- n1 + n2 − n3 − n4 = m2 (coefficient of φ),
- n1 − n2 + n3 − n4 = m3 (coefficient of ψ),
- n1 − n2 − n3 + n4 = m4 (struck out but implied).

This is a 4×4 Hadamard system, and he inverts it: 4 n1 = m1 + m2 + m3 + m4.

PURPOSE. The aim seems to be solving Δu = μ²u (a membrane/plate or eigenvalue-type problem) in a domain whose image under the elliptic map is a circle or annulus sector. This would be done by power series in r e^{iφ}.
- This is consistent with the neighbouring pages: the previous page has trigonometric eigenvalue conditions in √λ; the next page has double power series in p, q with coefficient recursions.
- It is plausibly connected with the boundary-value problems Riemann studied in the 1850s.
errors: First line, final sign: the correct result is ∫_0^a = −∫_∞^{1/(ak)} dy/√((1−y²)(1−k²y²)) = ∫_{1/(ak)}^∞ …. Riemann's final '+∫_∞^{1/(ak)}' has the wrong sign; the sign symbol appears struck or overwritten, perhaps a self-correction. (Branch-sign conventions for √ of negative quantities are left implicit.)
In the middle integral of the first line the second radical should be √(y²/k² − 1); the struck 'k²' was evidently a slip that Riemann corrected.

The line 'a = −1/(ak)' changes the involution from y ↦ 1/(ky) (used in the first line) to y ↦ −1/(ky). Both preserve the differential up to sign, but the switch is not commented on. With the minus sign the fixed points are ±i/√k, matching the next line.

The computation of the branch-point images (lines '(z − i/√k) ± …' and 'z(1 + i/√k) − …') is fragmentary scratch work and not carried through in writing. The final product form with roots ±e^{±φi} is nevertheless correct for the normalized variable w = −i√k z, with φ = 2 arctan(1/√k).
Passing from the quartic in z to √(z(z−e^{ψi})(z−e^{−ψi})) requires z → z², which drops a factor 1/2 and doubles the angle (ψ_new = 2ψ). This is not stated but is harmless.

The binomial-series line is partly illegible. The left form needs a factor (−1)^n Π(−1/2) to equal the right form Π(n−1/2)/(Πn Π(−1/2)), and the right form is correct. The expansions converge only for r < 1, i.e. inside the circle carrying the branch points.

Using a fourth combination m4 = n1 − n2 − n3 + n4 is a device; it is not an independent exponent of the product. Only m1, m2, m3 appear as exponents, so the inversion formula gives n1 in terms of m1, m2, m3 and the auxiliary m4.

results.what: Invariance of the Legendre differential dy/√((1−y²)(1−k²y²)) under y ↦ 1/(ky), and the resulting integral identity ∫_0^a = ∫_{1/(ak)}^∞
results.modern_name: Involution (automorphism) of the Legendre elliptic curve; reciprocal-modulus / inversion transformation of the elliptic integral

results.what: Möbius involution z = (i/√k)(y+i/√k)/(y−i/√k), sending the fixed points of y ↦ −1/(ky) to 0, ∞ and the branch points ±1, ±1/k to ±e^{±iφ}; the quartic becomes z⁴ − 2cos2φ z² + 1
results.modern_name: Möbius normalization of the elliptic curve to a symmetric quartic with roots on the unit circle (a symmetric normal form)
results.usually_credited_to: Classical (Jacobi/Legendre era); such normal forms appear in later texts

results.what: Conformal map ζ = ∫ dz/√(z(z−e^{iψ})(z−e^{−iψ})) and the transformation of Δu = μ²u to log-polar coordinates with conformal factor √(r²−2r cos(φ+ψ)+1)√(r²−2r cos(φ−ψ)+1)/r
results.modern_name: Conformal invariance of the Laplacian (Δ_ζ = |dL/dζ|² Δ_L); Schwarz–Christoffel-type elliptic mapping; Helmholtz/modified Helmholtz equation in conformal coordinates
results.usually_credited_to: Conformal change of the Laplacian: Gauss, Lamé, Riemann (1851). Schwarz–Christoffel formula: Christoffel (1867) and Schwarz (1869)

results.what: Expansion of the conformal factor as a product of four (1 − r e^{±i(φ±ψ)})^{−1/2} binomial series, with index bookkeeping by a Hadamard-type linear system and its inversion 4n1 = m1+m2+m3+m4
results.modern_name: Binomial series with Gauss's Π-function coefficients; Cauchy product of multiple series; inversion of a 4×4 Hadamard matrix

deep.surprise_reason: All the techniques are standard for the period and fit Riemann's known style: elliptic-integral substitutions, Möbius normalization, conformal transformation of the Laplacian, and binomial expansions in Gauss's Π notation. The mildly interesting detail is using an explicit elliptic conformal map to attack Δu = μ²u, a Helmholtz-type eigenvalue problem, in a non-trivial domain. In that it slightly anticipates a Schwarz–Christoffel-type approach, but the map is only set up, not exploited, and Riemann is already known for conformal-mapping methods.

checkable.asserts: The Möbius map z = (i/√k)(y+i/√k)/(y−i/√k) is an involution, so the inverse has the same form (Riemann's symmetric line −√k i y = (z+c)/(z−c)).

checkable.asserts: All three are zero: the branch points 1, −1, 1/k, −1/k map to e^{iφ}, e^{−iφ}, −e^{−iφ}, −e^{iφ} under w = −i√k z.
The image of y = 1 lies on the unit circle, so it can be written e^{iφ}.
Under y = c(w+1)/(w−1), the Legendre quartic (1−y²)(1−k²y²)·(w−1)⁴ is a constant multiple of w⁴ − 2cos(2φ)w² + 1. So dy/√Q(y) becomes const·dw/√(symmetric quartic).
≈ 0: ∫_0^a = ∫_{1/(ak)}^∞ for the Legendre integrand. This corrects the sign of Riemann's '+∫_∞^{1/(ak)}'.
Gives 0: |re^{iφ} − e^{iψ}|² = r² − 2r cos(φ−ψ) + 1, which yields the conformal factor in Riemann's line.

The binomial series 1 + x/2 + 3x²/8 + 5x³/16 + … matches Π(n−1/2)/(Πn Π(−1/2)).

transcription_corrections: Line 2: the image reads 'a = −1/(ak)' (with a minus sign), not 'a = 1/(ak)'. This is why the next line gives a = i/√k.
First line, middle integral: the second radical should read √(y²/k² − 1); the 'k²' after the minus sign is struck out in the manuscript.
First line, final equality: the sign before ∫_∞^{1/(ak)} is overwritten or struck (looks like a crossed '+').
Line '(z − i/√k) ± …': the manuscript reads roughly '(z − i/√k) = i/√k (z + i/√k) ± (z − i/√k) + z + i/√k'. It is scratch for the images of the branch points; the exact signs are uncertain.
The marks '− − +' under 'z(1 + i/√k) − i/√k(1 − i/√k)' and the small '+' above the product (z − e^{φi})… appear to be sign annotations for the four roots, not part of an equation.
Line 'x + y^i = ∫^{re^{φi}} dz/√(z(z − e^{ψi})(z − e^{−ψi}))' is correct as transcribed; the radical contains z times two factors.
In the conformal-factor line the denominator is r; the radicands are r² − 2cos(φ+ψ) r + 1 and r² − 2cos(φ−ψ) r + 1.
Binomial line: the left-hand side appears to read Σ e^{(φ+ψ)in} r^n (−1)^n Π(−1/2)/(Πn Π(−1/2−n)). The factors after r^n are hard to read, and the transcription's '…' hides the needed (−1)^n factor.
The struck fourth line of the linear system reads approximately 'n1 − n2 − n3 + n4 = m4'.
